title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The failure here is at the data-acquisition stage of model development. Suno admitted its model was trained on what it described as essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack identified YouTube, Deezer, and Genius among the specific sources scraped. Neither Suno nor Udio disclosed which works trained their models during litigation, which means the boundary between licensed and unlicensed material was not established before deployment. The system then produced outputs that, when given style-descriptive prompts, closely reproduced identifiable sections of specific recordings, showing that the training data influenced the generated output in directly traceable ways.

This is a case of a system deployed without rights clearance for its inputs and without output filtering sufficient to prevent near-reproduction of protected works. Catching it would have required either licensing agreements before training, a process for identifying and excluding protected works from training data, or post-generation screening that flagged outputs closely matching known recordings. None of those controls appears to have been in place. A German court found Suno liable in a case brought by the performing rights society GEMA, Warner Music reached a settlement with Suno and formed a joint venture, and Universal Music settled with Udio, but class actions from independent artists and a lawsuit from music publisher Round Hill remained active at the time of reporting.

What is not established is whether the training or the generation practices were intentional infringement rather than a disputed interpretation of fair use, which is the defense both companies have asserted. Lawsuits and a single court ruling in one jurisdiction are not a finding of intent, and the broader US litigation had not reached final verdicts as of the reporting gathered here.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, Capitol Records, and Atlantic Records, have sued two popular AI music generators called Udio and Suno. The labels accuse both companies of scraping thousands of copyrighted songs without permission to train their AI models and then generating new music that directly reproduces sections of famous recordings. The lawsuits were filed in New York against Udio and in Massachusetts against Suno, where the companies are based. The record labels submitted a massive list of thousands of specific copyrighted works they claim were used illegally, including songs from artists like The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Mariah Carey, and Bruce Springsteen.

To support their claims, the record labels demonstrated they could recreate famous songs by inputting specific prompts into both AI music generators. For example, using prompts describing Chuck Berry's style generated outputs that closely mimicked "Johnny B. Goode," and a prompt about Mariah Carey produced a near identical version of "All I Want for Christmas Is You." Both Udio and Suno have refused to disclose which music trained their models, claiming their use of copyrighted material constitutes fair use. The lawsuits represent a major legal battle about generative AI services and copyright protection.
